reasoning: lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. u = -30, f = +20. 1/v = 1/20 + 1/(-30) = 1/20 - 1/30. lcm 60 so (2-3)/60 = -1/60, v = -60 cm. negative so image is on the same side as the object

feedback: Your method is right: you used the lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f with correct signs (u = -30, f = +20), and you knew a negative v means the same side as the object. The slip is in the LCM step. 1/20 = 3/60 and 1/30 = 2/60, so the result is (3-2)/60 = +1/60, giving v = +60 cm, on the other side of the lens (option D). A quick check: an object between f and 2f of a convex lens gives a real image beyond 2f on the opposite side, so a virtual image on the object's side could not be right.

reasoning: angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the mirror, so the ray makes 40 deg with the first mirror and reflects at 40 deg with it too. mirrors are at 90 so in the triangle 180 - 90 - 40 = 50, so it hits the second mirror at 50 deg
knownLabels: Measures angles from the mirror surface
expectedMisconception: Measures angles from the mirror surface
gotMisconception: Measures angles from the mirror surface
evidence: angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the mirror, so the ray makes 40 deg with the first mirror
feedback: Your triangle idea is good: the two mirrors and the ray form a triangle with a 90° corner. But the angle of incidence is measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface. So 40° incidence means the ray makes 50° with mirror 1. The triangle then gives 180 - 90 - 50 = 40° with mirror 2, and the incidence angle there is 90 - 40 = 50°. You reached 50° only because two mix-ups cancelled. Check with a ray hitting a mirror head-on: its angle of incidence is 0°, though it makes 90° with the surface.

reasoning: fuse just has to be in series with the appliance, so in live or neutral both it would cut the current when it melts. live is the usual one so i chose live

gotMisconception: Fuse can go in the neutral wire
evidence: fuse just has to be in series with the appliance, so in live or neutral both it would cut the current when it melts. live is the usual one so i chose live
feedback: You are right that a fuse must be in series and that it cuts the current when it melts. But it matters which wire: if the fuse is in the neutral, the appliance stays connected to the live wire after the fuse blows. The metal body can then stay at high potential, and a person touching it can get a shock. Live is not just 'usual'; it is the safe choice because a blown fuse in the live wire disconnects the appliance completely from the high potential.

feedback: You are right that the current is the same all the way round, so A is the correct option. But the reason is wrong: the cell does not make charge and the lamp does not destroy it. The charge is already in the wire, and the cell only pushes it around the loop. Because charge cannot pile up or vanish anywhere, the same amount passes every point each second. Quick check: a wire has the same number of charges in it before and after you switch on the circuit.
